beats.text: Okay, so we've all been through. You're talking to somebody, you know, close enough to see their teeth, and then all of a sudden they lean away and you're like, wait a second, is my breath stink? Is it me?
beats.note: Okay, so we've all been through it (Ben, 2026-09-28: keep 'we've all been there'); leaning away; is my breath stink? Is it me?

beats.text: You're like, if I do have that breath, how do I get rid of it? Because to be honest, who's gonna ever tell me really?
beats.note: how do I get rid of it; who's gonna ever tell me (the long loop)

beats.text: And the crazy part is you're actually really bad at smelling your own breath. Everybody really is. It's, I mean, it's the same thing as like you walk into somebody's house and they're just used to the way that their house smells. They don't really know that their house smelled bad. It's the same thing with your mouth.
beats.note: bad at smelling your own breath; the house analogy

beats.text: And most people think that they got bad breath from something that they ate, you know, like the garlic and all that type of stuff, but that's not quite true. Because trust me, I'm an orthodontist. I've been in people's mouths all the time. I know what bad breath smells like. And more than likely, it's actually your mouth, like eight or nine times out of ten. It's gonna be your mouth rather than something you ate.
beats.note: not what you ate; trust me I'm an orthodontist; 8 or 9 out of 10 (stat 1)

beats.text: And it's actually super common.
beats.note: super common (S034 retake dropped)

beats.text: About one in three people have bad breath or halitosis. So if that's you, you're definitely not alone.
beats.note: 1 in 3 (stat 2); not alone

beats.text: So the real question is, how do you check something that you can't even smell? And where is it really coming from? Because, because I don't think it's where most people think it comes from.
beats.note: the real question; where is it coming from (loop 2). S041 dropped: the title card lands here

beats.text: So first off, the reason that you can't smell your own bad breath is because, well, your nose gets used to smells around you that are frequent. It kind of just stops noticing it all together. And trust me, there's nothing more around you than your bad breath. I mean, literally, it's coming out of your face all day long. And this whole, like, cup your hand over your mouth and snippet thing, that doesn't really work either. You're kind of just smelling the same air that you've been smelling all day long.
beats.note: nose gets used to it; coming out of your face all day; cupping your hand doesn't work

beats.text: And people have actually tested how good we are at this.
beats.note: people have tested this

beats.text: They had people that were worried about their breath, rate their own breath, you know, the smell of it, and then they would have a professional bad breath smeller, yeah, that's actually a thing, apparently it's their job to just smell bad breath, would smell it and then rate it, and guess what?
beats.note: the study: self-rating vs a professional smeller ... and guess what?

beats.text: people only got it right like half of the time,
beats.note: people only got it right like half of the time (stat 3; 'they almost always got it wrong' dropped: the study found 38% agreement, so 'almost always wrong' overstates it)

beats.text: but there is something you can do. It is kind of gross, but basically what you want to do is you want to lick your wrist, and then what you're gonna do is you're gonna wait for about 10 seconds for it to dry, and then while that's dry, then you're going to smell it.
beats.note: there is something you can do: lick your wrist, 10 seconds, smell it

beats.text: so go ahead and do that right now. I'll wait.

beats.text: Okay, so if it smells bad, well, that's probably what people are getting when you talk to them. Sorry. And if it didn't, well, that doesn't totally mean that you're in the clear. Because your wrist is really only getting the stuff that's on the tip of the tongue, not the rest. And the tip is usually the cleanest part of your entire tongue.

beats.text: You know, it's mainly because it's rubbing across your teeth all the time, the roof of your mouth.

beats.text: Water and saliva is always hitting it and stuff like that.
beats.note: water and saliva always hitting it

beats.text: That's why when a dentist checks you for real, they go all the way to the back. Scrape that off with their little mirror, let it dry, and then smell that.
beats.note: a dentist checks the back: scrape with the mirror, let it dry, smell

beats.text: So this leads us to the back of the tongue. If you look at a tongue close up microscopically, it's not smooth at all. It's actually covered by these tiny little bumps. And as you go further back, weirdly enough, they get longer and longer. It's almost like those old shag carpets you've seen, you know, all the shag moving around. And just like that real shag carpet, well, food, gunk, particles, all that get stuck in between those little shag carpet filaments. And not only just food, but you have mucus and dead cells from your cheek and tongue. And spit can't really get all the way down there to wash it all out either. And guess what? The bacteria, they absolutely love it down there.
beats.note: the back of the tongue: bumps get longer, shag carpet, gunk, mucus, dead cells, spit can't reach, bacteria love it

beats.text: And fun fact, they're the kind that actually don't even like oxygen. And guess what? Not a lot of oxygen down there. So technically it's the perfect spot for those bacteria to live. And then what they do is they eat all that gunk, the dead cells, the proteins, and mucus, all that, they eat it up.
beats.note: don't like oxygen (last take S079); perfect spot; they eat the gunk

beats.text: and some of that stuff, specifically proteins, have sulfur in them.
beats.note: some of that stuff, specifically proteins, have sulfur (second take)

beats.text: So when the bacteria eat that and then they will poop out their remains, well, they poop out sulfur gas. We actually call these volatile sulfur compounds. And one of the main ones is the same gas that makes that rotten egg smell.
beats.note: poop out sulfur gas; volatile sulfur compounds; rotten egg

beats.text: Basically what you're smelling is the remains of the leftovers, that bacteria basically dissolve and poop out on your mouth.
beats.note: what you're smelling is the leftovers bacteria poop out (the gross-out line)

beats.text: And the fun fact is, you can see it. That's right. If you stick your tongue out and it's super white, yellow, or you know, sometimes even black if it gets really crazy, that's what we call a coated tongue. And that's probably where your bad breath is coming from.
beats.note: you can see it: coated tongue; that's probably where it's coming from

beats.text: And you really, you think it would be your teeth because that's what we've been told our whole lives. But there's this bad breath clinic over in Belgium. There's this periodontist named Mark Quirion and Yeah, I completely botched that. But they have this whole clinic just for breath.
beats.note: you'd think teeth; the Belgium clinic; Marc Quirynen, 'I completely botched that' (kept: human, gets a correct-spelling card)

beats.text: and they went through like 2,000 patients.
beats.note: and they went through like 2,000 patients (stat 4)

beats.text: And the number one cause of bad breath they found was just the coating on the tongue. It was way more than, you know, gum problems or anything they found with teeth.
beats.note: number one cause: tongue coating, way more than gums or teeth

beats.text: And a good chunk,
beats.note: And a good chunk, (spliced to the second take's 'of people...')

beats.text: of people didn't even have bad breath. They were just really worried that they did.
beats.note: of people didn't even have bad breath, just worried

beats.text: Now the other spots in your mouth are kind of the same idea. In between your teeth, the food gets stuck there, they get bacteria, breaks it down, and you know, yada, yada, yada. You know, eventually the gum gets inflamed, bone disease, gum disease, all that type of stuff happens. And some of those gum disease bacteria actually make that same sulfur breakdown smell as well. So bad breath that won't go away no matter what you do can also be a sign of gum disease, technically. And if you got braces, oh my gosh, it's it's even worse because there were so many little spots for that food and gum to just get all over those brackets.
beats.note: between teeth, gum disease, same sulfur smell, warning sign; braces

beats.text: And another thing, your spit is also a really big part of this. You see saliva is basically the power washer of your mouth. It's what's washing things down all day long. And unfortunately, when you sleep, that saliva amount slows way down. I think that's probably pretty much why you wake up with bad breath in the morning for the most part. And if you sleep with an open mouth, well, it gets even worse because now you're drying out the already dry area. And even worse, if you're on medications that dry your mouth out on top of that.
beats.note: saliva power washer; sleep; morning breath; open mouth; medications

beats.text: Now, if you keep going past your tongue, we reach another spot of bad breathification, and that is the tonsil stones. You see, your tonsils have these little holes in them. We call them tonsillar crips. And guess what? Yes, food and gum can also get stuck up in there. And every time you swallow, they get squished down and compacted into these tight little balls of nastiness called tonsil stones. It's literally rotten food, basically, just stuck in your mouth that you can't get out. It's pretty bad. And trust me, these ones, they smell different. They smell a whole world of different. if you've ever grabbed a tonsil stone, smished it in your mouth and smelled it, you know exactly what I'm talking about. It's not good. And I can, I can, I can, and I can tell if someone has tonsil stones a mile away. It's a way different smell.
beats.note: tonsil crypts, compacted stones, rotten food; they smell different; a mile away

beats.text: And the crazy part is a lot of people have these, they got no idea. There was actually a study that looked at these on CT scans and they found that one in four people actually have tonsil stones just walking around. But I would say that probably this, the slice, although they are a definite cause of bad breath, it seems like from the research that tongue coating and bacteria is a bigger cause of that bad breath on average.
beats.note: lots of people have them; CT study 1 in 4 (stat 5); a smaller slice than tongue coating

beats.text: So it is definitely something to look out for.
beats.note: something to look out for (S138 'no matter what' and S139 repeat dropped)

beats.text: Now we've gone for the teeth and the mouth and tongues all the way back to the tonsils. Well, let's keep going back into the throat now. And the question is, is like, wait, is there bad breath coming from my stomach? Is what I eat actually a big deal? And well, kind of a little bit. Because it's not actually coming from the food, it's probably coming from the stomach, and that stomach is acid reflux. Technically, sinuses can do it too, it can drain down from your sinuses into the back of your throat, as well, that is another thing that can happen. And there is another thing too, if you're diabetic or something like that, if you have a lot of ketones on your breath, your breath can actually still smell sweet, not necessarily bad though. But your stomach is not breathing out of your mouth all the time, there's a little valve that literally holds all of those things in, so it doesn't really make sense to go through your mouth. So unless you have reflux, more than likely it's coming from your mouth.
beats.note: down the throat: is it my stomach? reflux, sinuses, diabetes ketones, the valve, so it's your mouth (S151 comment ask dropped)

beats.text: now that we know where bad breath comes from, what next? You've had breath, you've had bad breath for a while, you've tried everything. You've tried mints, and mouthwash, and brushing harder.
beats.note: now that we know where it comes from, what next? mints, mouthwash, brushing harder

beats.text: And the reason that none of it's really worked is because,
beats.note: and the reason none of it's really worked is because,

beats.text: you see, a mint just covers up your breath for a few minutes.
beats.note: you see, a mint just covers up your breath for a few minutes

beats.text: And fun fact, if that mint is actually sugary, well, that bacteria is still in your mouth. And guess what? That bacteria eat sugar. So you're actually feeding that bacteria
beats.note: a sugary mint: bacteria eat sugar, you're feeding that bacteria (ends before 'to create more VSCs': research row 14, the sulfur-makers eat protein; graphic shows cavity bacteria)

beats.text: And most mouthwash, to be honest, are kind of doing the same thing as well. And brushing harder, like I said, you know, that deals mainly with the teeth. You can brush the tongue as well, but if you're just kind of moving things around, you're not really doing as much as you really need to to get it off.
beats.note: mouthwash same; brushing harder mostly the teeth

beats.text: Because it's not like if you have that breath, you're not cleaning your mouth or taking care of your mouth. It's probably a little different than that. I mean, more likely, you're probably doing what you're doing. You're probably brushing, you're probably flossing. It's just that you're not doing exactly what you need to do to get rid of that bad breath. And you're not actually cleaning the one spot that, you know, most people don't ever clean.
beats.note: it's not that you're not cleaning; you're missing the one spot (S166 'misnomer' dropped)

beats.text: Now, to be fair, I don't want to oversell this. The research on fixing bad breath is honestly not great. There's a ton of small studies, and even big studies, I looked at all the small studies, really just kind of said that everything was kind of weak,
beats.note: to be fair: research not great, studies weak

beats.text: And if you're thinking about a tongue scraper specifically, I'm sure most of you guys are. The studies do say that using a tongue scraper is better than a toothbrush, but not by much. And the problem is, is it wears right off, in that, you know, the coating just comes right back. So it's something that you have to do every single day.
beats.note: tongue scraper better than a toothbrush but not by much; wears off; every day

beats.text: And then obviously we have the alcohol mouthwash thing. I definitely wouldn't use alcohol mouthwash if I was you, you know, because it can dry out your mouth even more. And even more importantly, it can kill some of the good bacteria that fight those bacteria that cause those volatile salt for compounds. So try and find, you know if you know, an alcohol free mouthwash if you are going to go to that root.
beats.note: alcohol mouthwash (Ben's recommendation; research row 13 says the evidence is mixed: flagged)

beats.text: So I'm not necessarily saying cleaning your tongue is some miracle way to just completely get rid of your bad breath, but it doesn't hurt. And so it's cheap, it's easy, and so I would recommend doing it if you can and you have access to doing that.
beats.note: not a miracle, but it doesn't hurt; cheap, easy (S186 'not really going to solve your bad breath' dropped: contradicts the payoff)

beats.text: So what actually works? Well, if you came and asked me, I mean, obviously the easy one is like, yeah, just start tongue scraping.
beats.note: so what actually works? start tongue scraping

beats.text: At least get the gunk and nastiness off of your tongue, off of your gums, off of your teeth. Do all the things that you're supposed to be doing.
beats.note: get the gunk off your tongue, gums, teeth; do all the things

beats.text: You want to literally go make sure when you're doing this, go as far back as you can, scrape everything off and get everything off there, rinse it off, and do it multiple times until you stop getting that gunk off of your mouth. If you are a big gagger and you just feel you can't get too far back, well then start a little bit in the middle of your tongue and then slowly work your way you get used to that. But the goal is we really want to clean that area good.
beats.note: go as far back as you can; gagger tip

beats.text: Now obviously you want to clean between your teeth and floss every day because that same bacteria is sitting inside in between all those nooks and crannies, also breaking down all that food. And if you have dry mouth, well make sure if you're going to use mince do like a xylitol mint or something like that instead of a sugary mint. because like I said, you're just going to feed that bacteria with the sugary stuff as well.
beats.note: floss daily; xylitol mint instead of sugary

beats.text: If these bacteria are the problem and doing all these things in the studies, like it helps, but it's like it's not the end game because it just keeps coming back, what do you do?

beats.text: But what if I told you that we actually, at something nice, my own company, created a way to deal with this that has never been done in the history of dentistry.

beats.text: This is really cool biotech that can actually specifically target certain bacteria.
beats.note: biotech that targets certain bacteria

beats.text: Everything comes back to these bacteria that break down the food, release these volatile sulfur compounds. And we target one of these main bacteria that causes this, which is P. gingivalis. It's one of the biggest bacteria that causes those volatile sulfur compounds.

beats.text: Because what we've done is we've taken that activated oil system, those nano lipid emulsions and we've actually put it in our toothpaste, and it's called Zero Pro.

beats.text: And you can actually get this today, which is really, really crazy. It actually took us two years development We have a universally backed double blind human study on this, so yes, it is all there, it is all true, and it actually does work.
beats.note: and you can actually get this today... took us two years (of) development... we have a (university-)backed double blind human study on this, so yes, it is all there, it is all true, and it actually does work (Ben's note at 10:55: the pitch needs this; claims are his, flagged for his confirmation)

beats.text: What it does it basically seeks it out, attaches to it, and then pops it. Like a water balloon. And the cool thing is, unlike alcohol mouthwrenches that harm all the bacteria that they've got, this only specifically kills the bacteria that we target.
